description: Shani Shingnapur is a village in Newasa taluka of Ahilyanagar (formerly Ahmednagar) district, built around a shrine to Shani, the deity associated with the planet Saturn. The object of worship is a tall, self-emerged black stone that stands on an open platform with no roof, since the deity is said to prefer the open sky. According to local tradition, a shepherd came upon the stone and Shani later appeared to him in a dream, asking for regular worship. The village is also known for houses and shops with door frames but no doors or locks, a custom residents attribute to the deity's protection. The temple is managed by Shri Shanaishwar Devasthan, reconstituted under a 2018 Maharashtra Act.

description: Saptashrungi Devi Temple lies near Vani and Nanduri in Kalwan taluka of Nashik district, roughly 60 km from Nashik city, on a hill of the Sahyadri range encircled by seven peaks. The goddess, worshipped as a form of Durga, is a figure about eight feet tall with eighteen arms, each holding a different weapon, carved in relief from the natural rock face. Many sources, including government tourism pages, count the shrine as the ardha (half) Shakti Peetha among the 'three and a half' in Maharashtra, though the temple's own site and some other sources describe it as a full peetha. Pilgrims reach it by a stairway of about 510 steps, reportedly built in 1710, or by a funicular that opened in 2018. The major fairs fall during Chaitra and the Ashwin Navaratri period.

description: Akkalkot, in Solapur district, is the main centre of devotion to Swami Samarth, a nineteenth-century saint whom followers regard as an incarnation of Dattatreya. He is traditionally said to have come to the town in 1856 and stayed there for roughly two decades, until he took samadhi in 1878. He lived in the house of his disciple Cholappa, where the Samadhi Math stands. The Vatavruksh Mandir complex is built around the banyan tree under which he is said to have sat and taught; a tradition holds that he described himself as born of a banyan. The temple complex includes a sabha mandap and accommodation, free meals are served twice daily, and his death anniversary is observed each year on Chaitra Shuddha Trayodashi.

description: Alandi, on the Indrayani river in Pune district, is the samadhi shrine of Sant Dnyaneshwar, the thirteenth-century Marathi saint who composed the Dnyaneshwari, a Marathi commentary on the Bhagavad Gita, and is counted among the founders of the Varkari tradition. According to Wikipedia, he entered sanjeevan samadhi in 1296 beneath the Siddheshwar temple complex, which also contains the Ajanvriksha tree. A temple over the samadhi is dated to roughly 1580 to 1600, with later additions by Maratha nobles, the Peshwa and the Shinde family. Press reports say a 22 kg gold kalash, handed to the Sant Dnyaneshwar Maharaj Sansthan Committee, was placed atop the samadhi temple in August 2025. Each year the saint's padukas travel from Alandi to Pandharpur in the Wari procession.

description: Ballaleshwar at Pali, in Raigad district, is one of the eight Ashtavinayak Ganesha shrines and is unusual in being named after a devotee, Ballal, rather than the deity. According to tradition, Ballal, a merchant's son, was punished by his father for worshipping Ganesha with village children; Ganesha then appeared and agreed to remain in Pali in the stone bearing the devotee's name. The broken stone is worshipped as Dhundi Vinayak. The devasthan's history page describes restoration of an older temple from about 1751 under Baburao Phadnis, a sabhamandap built between 1902 and 1908, and repairs in the early 1930s. Wikipedia describes an east-facing temple between Sarasgad fort and the Amba river. Visitors should confirm current darshan and aarti timings with the devasthan, as they can change on festival days.

description: The Varadvinayak temple stands beside a lake at Mahad village in Khalapur taluka, Raigad district, and is counted among the eight Ashtavinayak Ganesha shrines of Maharashtra. Ganesha is worshipped here as Varadvinayak in an image that devotees regard as self-manifested (swayambhu) and that faces east with its trunk curving to the left. According to tradition, the image was found submerged in the neighbouring lake in 1690, and according to Wikipedia the present temple was built or restored in 1725 by the Peshwa-era sardar Ramji Mahadev Biwalkar. Four elephant figures guard the temple's sides, and the complex also holds images of Mushika, the Navagraha and a Shivalinga. Wikipedia adds that devotees may enter the sanctum to worship the idol directly, and that large crowds gather for Magha Chaturthi.

description: Mahaganapati Temple at Ranjangaon, in Shirur taluka of Pune district about 50 km from Pune, is one of the eight Ashtavinayak shrines of Maharashtra, where Ganesha is worshipped as Mahaganapati. The east-facing temple has a large entrance gate topped by a nagarkhana (drum house).

description: Nageshwar Jyotirlinga Temple lies on the Saurashtra coast in Devbhumi Dwarka district, roughly 16 to 18 km from Dwarka city, depending on the source. It is dedicated to Shiva as Nageshwar and is counted among the twelve Jyotirlingas. According to the associated legend, the demon Daruka imprisoned the devotee Supriya, whose chanting of Shiva's name brought the god to defeat him. Tourism pages describe a large hall leading to the sanctum, an underground sanctum holding the lingam, and an 80-foot seated statue of Shiva at the site. Gopi Talav Tirth is nearby, and Maha Shivaratri is the festival most often cited. The Nageshwar claim is also made for Aundha in Maharashtra and Jageshwar in Uttarakhand, and Wikipedia says the location of Darukavana remains debated.

description: Shamlaji, in Gujarat's Aravalli district, is a Vishnu temple on the bank of the Meshwo river, in a valley ringed by wooded hills. The black image of the deity is worshipped as Gadadhar, a name linked to the mace he holds, and local tribal communities also revere him as Kaliyo Dev, the Dark Divine. According to Wikipedia, the present building mainly dates from the 15th to 16th centuries, though construction may have begun around the 11th century, and the sanctum sculpture is probably much older, perhaps 7th to 8th century. Gujarat Tourism describes a two-storey structure of white sandstone and brick, with scenes from the Ramayana and Mahabharata carved on its outer walls. Devotees also bathe in the river, and a large annual fair is held at Kartik Purnima.

Pilgrims climb a long flight of steps to reach the shrine on the summit.

description: Mehandipur Balaji temple in Dausa district, Rajasthan, is dedicated to Hanuman, worshipped here as Balaji. According to local lore, the image manifested miraculously in the hills; no founding date or builder is firmly documented. Alongside Balaji, the sanctum is described as holding representations of Pret Raj Sarkar and Kotwal Bhairav. The temple is best known for a tradition among devotees that attending darshan and following its rituals brings relief from what they understand as spirit affliction, and from mental and physical distress. These are matters of belief rather than established fact, and the temple's practices have also been the subject of academic and psychiatric study. The Ghata Mehandipur Balaji Trust is reported to run education, health and welfare work. Pilgrims come from Rajasthan and elsewhere throughout the year.

description: Mahur, in the Sahyadri foothills of Nanded district and also called Mahurgad, is the seat of Goddess Renuka, mother of Parashurama in Hindu tradition. The temple is counted among the Shakta pithas of Maharashtra, and tradition holds that it marks the spot where her head fell; the shrine is described as housing a self-manifested image of which only the head is visible. According to the Nanded district website, a Yadava king of Devgiri built it roughly 800 to 900 years ago. The town is also revered as the birthplace of Dattatreya, with a shrine on Datta Shikhar, the highest of its three hills. Pilgrims climb stone steps to the hilltop shrines, and a large fair is held each year at Dasara.

description: Dehu, on the Indrayani river in Pune district, is the home village of Sant Tukaram, the 17th-century Marathi Warkari poet-saint remembered for abhang verses addressed to Vitthal. The village temple stands on the riverbank and is managed by the Jagatguru Sant Shri Tukaram Maharaj Sansthan. The complex includes the Shila Mandir, a stone shrine linked to the rock on which, according to tradition, he sat for thirteen days when his abhangs were challenged; the Prime Minister inaugurated it in June 2022. The nearby Gatha Mandir has about 4,000 of his abhangs carved on its walls, and the Tukaram Palkhi procession to Pandharpur sets out from Dehu in the month of Ashadh, making it a major Warkari pilgrimage place.

description: The Elephanta Caves are a group of seven rock-cut cave excavations on Elephanta Island, also called Gharapuri, in Mumbai harbour (administratively in Raigad district, Maharashtra). They are a UNESCO World Heritage Site protected by the Archaeological Survey of India. Cave 1, the largest, is devoted to Shiva. Its entrance is dominated by a sculpture about 7 metres high, Sadashiva, showing three aspects of the god, and panels include Ardhanarishvara, Nataraja, Gangadhara and Shiva and Parvati playing chausar. Cave 1 measures 39 metres from front to back and its plan resembles Dumar Lena at Ellora. The ASI dates the caves to roughly the 6th-7th centuries CE, while UNESCO gives the mid-5th to 6th centuries. The island is named after a colossal elephant statue now kept in Jijamata Garden, Mumbai.

description: The Amba Mata temple stands on the first peak of Girnar, the hill above Junagadh that carries both Hindu and Jain shrines. Gujarat Tourism says newly married couples come here to pray for a happy marriage. The shrine is also known as the Ambika (Ambaji) temple; in Jain tradition Ambika is a yakshini attending the 22nd Tirthankara, Neminatha, and the shrine is visited by both Hindu and Jain pilgrims. The present building is dated to about the 15th century. An inscription of 1192 CE records a pilgrimage by the minister Vastupala, and a 1468 CE eulogy credits the merchant Samal Sah with renovating it. A ropeway, inaugurated in October 2020, rises to the temple; the full climb to the highest peak, Neminath Shikhar, is about 10,000 stone steps.

description: The Hutheesing Jain Temple, also called Hathisingh Derasar, is a white marble Shvetambara Jain temple outside Delhi Darwaza in Shahibaug, Ahmedabad. Its main sanctuary is dedicated to Dharmanatha, the 15th Tirthankara. It was completed in 1848. Hathisinh Kesarisinh, an Ahmedabad businessman, began it partly to give work to artisans in a famine; he died during construction and his wife, Harkunvar, completed it. The work is attributed to Premchand Salat. A pillared cloister around the courtyard holds 52 subsidiary shrines with marble images, and a Manastambha tower with a Mahavira statue stands in front. The temple is known for its rainwater harvesting arrangement, and Ahmedabad's municipal heritage page describes it as the largest Jain temple in the city.

description: Kesariyaji, also called Rishabhdev or Kesariyanath, is a temple at Rishabhdeo (Dhulev) in Udaipur district. Its black stone image of Rishabhanatha, the first Jain Tirthankara, is about 3.5 feet tall and seated in padmasana. The name Kesariya comes from the large quantity of saffron offered to the deity. Jains of both Shvetambara and Digambara traditions visit, and local Bhil and Meena communities also revere the image, with Bhils calling it Kalaji or Kalababa. According to tradition, a Bhil man named Dhula found the idol. The complex has 52 shrines. Its origins are not firmly established; sources give a date around the 9th century, and the site is often described as about 1,200 years old.

description: Shila Devi is a form of the goddess Durga, worshipped in a Shakta temple at Amer Fort near Jaipur and counted among the region's prominent Shakti shrines. The image is carved from stone, which gives the deity her name. According to tradition, Maharaja Man Singh I was blessed by the goddess in a dream and brought a stone slab from eastern Bengal; the slab was then carved into the image. Sources disagree on the founding date, giving 1580 and 1604. The Devasthan Department describes carved pillars and panels, a sanctum with four verandahs, and regular recitation of the Durga Saptashati. Special worship is held during Navaratri in Ashwin and Chaitra, when the temple draws large numbers of devotees.

description: Jeen Mata is a form of Shakti worshipped in a hill temple in the Aravalli range, in Sikar district. The Devasthan Department describes the image as Mahishasura Mardini Durga with eight arms and gives the construction date as unknown, citing a stone inscription as evidence of age. Local belief links the site to a woman named Jeen who practised austerity here and to the Pandavas' exile; a popular tradition holds that the temple is about 1,200 years old. The sanctum is marble with silver shutters, and a 24-pillared hall and tall shikhar follow Pratihara and Chauhan styles. A Bhramari Devi shrine stands behind. Devotees visit on the bright eighth of each month, bring infants for a first hair-cutting rite, and gather in large numbers at Chaitra and Ashwin Navaratri.
